beta_new: The route comprises three ridge sections separated by deep notches. The lower section is mostly class 2-4 terrain, commonly simul-climbed, staying just on the east side of the crest (harder climbing results if the crest itself is followed). After descending to the second notch, two 5.8 pitches (a dirty 5.8 chimney and a 5.8 crack pitch) lead toward the summit, separated by class 2-3 sections, with large detached blocks making protection difficult in places. A gendarme partway up offers the route's best technical climbing directly, or can be bypassed via a ~75-ft rappel to easier terrain west of the ridge.

From the col between Mount Stuart and Sherpa Peak, ascend the ridge generally trending climber's left. With a 60m rope you can reach the first belay in a cave-like feature with a platform large enough for several climbers; the crux is the crack leading out of the cave (rated 5.4-5.5). A second pitch leads to another anchor, after which a short 4th-class scramble gains the notoriously airy summit block.

moves.from: Descent is about four rappels down the ascent line, three single-rope and a final double-rope rappel to the west notch.

beta_new: Good feet throughout with one pumpy crux section that loads the arms; the difficulty here is more mental than physical since bolts are spaced roughly every four feet. The basalt climbs differently than Pinto Rock's typical knobby welded tuff, with a character closer to Exit 38. Best cleaned by the second since it's a lateral traverse.

Approach as for the Silver Star Glacier route to gain the glacier, then break off toward the northeast side of the west summit to climb the ridge/face directly rather than finishing via the standard scramble line. Beckey's 1952 party made the first recorded ascent of the west summit via this general northeast aspect from the glacier.

Start up the descent gully used for Gato Negro on adjacent Whine Spire, then follow the couloir; the first obstacle is a chockstone going at M2-3, followed by simulclimbing to a rightward fork and a crux chockstone requiring M4 climbing with minimal to no protection.

Climb a direct line up the consistent 45-50 degree névé and ice, deviating only briefly to skirt the bergschrund, until the angle eases near the top and a short rock/snow scramble leads to the summit.

moves.from: From a col south of Sinister, descend onto the Chickamin Glacier and traverse to the base of the north face at its lowest point.

beta_new: Approach via Downey Creek Trail to high camp at Cub Lake or Itswoot Ridge (5,400-6,400 ft). Traverse Chickamin Glacier to Dome-Sinister col at approximately 8,450 feet. Contour around Sinister's south side via easy snowfield, then climb a prominent loose gully (Class 3, loose rock) to the ridge. Ascend the upper west ridge via Class 2-3 snow and scrambling to the roomy summit. Total time from camp approximately 3-4 hours. The southwest gully is notably loose—exceptionally loose and unpleasant to climb. Descent can reverse via the gully or traverse to the lower west ridge (white-knuckle Class 3-4 scrambling with fixed sling protection at one crux).

Pitch 1 climbs a narrow 'whale's back' of stone between facing corners on polished friction, protected by nine bolts, and holds the route's crux. Subsequent pitches ease to 5.4-5.6 with occasional 5.8 sections. The final pitch features clean splitter cracks (5.7) finishing on the buttress crest with views over Whitehorse Mountain.

From the Stevens Pass parking area, a route climbs past a small gray WSDOT building, under powerlines, and up a gated gravel road to Skyline Lake, then ascends northwest through timber and open slopes to a gap in the Skyline Ridge crest before following the ridge, traversing below rocky sub-points, to the summit.

moves.from: A faint climbers' path parallels much of the gravel-road approach and is faster than the road.

beta_new: This is a two-pitch alpine rock climb that functions as a half-day objective after the long approach. Pitch 1 involves a low 5th class move followed by class 3 scrambling to a large tree belay (40 feet). Pitch 2 features face climbing transitioning to a gully, then exposed slab to the summit (50+ feet). The route can be climbed as one full 60m pitch or broken into two for better communication. A climbing register is present at the summit. Despite its name, this route is neither slippery nor a slab.

From either the Bedal Creek or Cougar Creek (North Fork Sauk) trailhead, a climber's trail leaves the maintained tread and climbs through forest and talus to a saddle near Bedal Peak, then crosses the Sloan Glacier. Parties step off the glacier at the Southeast ridge and follow a boot path that corkscrews south then north around the South ridge, finishing with a short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble to the summit.

From the junction, continue past a roughly 50-ft waterfall to an open meadow between Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, then switchback up open southwest-facing slopes to the summit. Most parties treat it as a there-and-back half-day trip; it is popular as both a snow-free scramble and, with an ice axe/crampons, a winter/spring snow climb.

moves.from: From the Snow Lake trailhead at Alpental, find an unsigned boot path just off an old dirt road. The path climbs a steep, loose creek bed through forest for about a mile to a junction (right forks to Guye Peak/Cave Ridge; stay left/straight for the summit).

beta_new: Traverse south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump onto the Colonial Glacier, climb ~30-degree snow to the Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,840 ft), then descend roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier. Rope up and cross the Neve — parties describe the cleanest line through the center of its crevasse field — to the ridge near The Horseman on Snowfield's west side (~7,700 ft), then finish with roughly 400-600 ft of class 3-4 (occasionally class 5 on variant lines) rock scrambling to the summit.

moves.from: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead, hike the well-worn trail to Pyramid Lake (~2 mi), then follow a steep, less-traveled climbers' trail up the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak into alpine terrain.

beta_new: This is the most-used of Snowking's standard lines and the one essentially every documented party takes, chosen for its directness, though it starts low (about 2,300 ft) and doesn't tour the whole mountain. Most groups treat it as a two-day trip with a bivy near Cyclone Lake, though strong parties have done it car-to-car in a long day (9-14 hrs) on firm spring snow. It is glacier travel, not technical climbing — ice axe, crampons, and a rope with basic crevasse-rescue gear are standard, and parties are advised to stay roped through the upper snowfield/glacier, especially once blue ice and crevasses open up in high summer.

value.text: Ice axe, crampons, and a rope with basic crevasse-rescue gear.

moves.from: ice axe, crampons, and a rope with basic crevasse-rescue gear are standard

beta_new: Ascend the prominent East Buttress via mixed rock and bolt-ladder terrain. Route is largely 5.8-5.9 with two crux pitches of 5.11 and one 5.10 connector. Bolt ladders on pitches 4 and 6 allow grade flexibility; many parties now free-climb the route entirely at 5.11.

Two-pitch technical rock climb on solid granite. The South Face receives consistent sun, making it a good choice early and late in the season. Approach via Burgundy Col from Highway 20. Descent via North Ridge scramble or rappel.

Follows the obvious weakness — the only reasonable passage — up the south face toward the bunny-ear notch on good cracks with solid protection, through a right-facing corner, finishing on a splitter thin-hands pitch on excellent granite before an A0 aid move off a bolt to reach the summit.

The easiest of Concord's standard routes. Start with a class-2 walk across gravelly, gently down-sloping ledges to the first belay, then climb up and right toward trees. A roped scramble along the ridge crest leads to a sandy stance near a feature climbers call the 'shark fin.' The final pitch climbs up and over the shark fin and onto the summit block, belaying from bolts at the top. Rock quality and protection are good throughout.

A long, alpine-feeling line with sections where rock quality and protection vary considerably; route-finding is non-trivial and some sections carry real fall consequences. Far less traveled than the North or Northwest Faces.

Follows the obvious crack in the middle of the south face wall starting from the notch: climb through a bulge, then trend left through two right-facing corners to a tree just below the summit block. At 220 feet, the whole route goes in one pitch with a 70m rope (or can be broken into two with a 60m rope). The route wanders, so expect to place extra alpine draws to manage rope drag; some loose blocks and flakes are present and the rock carries lichen from relatively light traffic.
Pitch 1 climbs 15 feet of 5.7 to a tree; subsequent pitches traverse ledges, include a chimney with a 5.6 downclimb, a 5.7 flake with stemming, and scrambling through boulders and trees to the top.

moves.from: From Edward Mesa (the 'Lost World Plateau'), descend to the south side of the peak to a steep gully marked by a giant chockstone.

beta_new: Crux is negotiating one or two chockstones jammed in the gully -- parties are typically forced left onto the adjacent face (or stem/squeeze past on sometimes wet, loose rock) before regaining the gully and following the South Spur to the top. Protection is sparse and low-5th-class: a small rack of cams and nuts plus slung trees, with a hand line sometimes rigged over the exposed ground above the chockstones.

5.8 YDS / VI- UIAA Grade II Alpine. 5 pitches trad climbing with 4–5 technical pitches. Two 20–30 ft sections of 5.7; extensive 4th–5th class scrambling. Hazards: frequent rockfall, loose rock/choss, exposure, early-season snow/ice. Best June–August (peak July); avoid late season. First Ascent: Myhre & Sorenson (1966).

Initial pitches climb 4th-class rock with gear available in a central dihedral; higher pitches are dirt/tree/talus gullies broken by 3rd-class steps, commonly simul-climbed. Rock quality is intermittent throughout.

From a camp at Wing Lake, hike around the lake and up a moraine onto a permanent snowfield to an obvious col in the south ridge. A broad, loose gully on the west side of the ridge leads up toward the final summit blocks, where several class-3 lines can be pieced together to a small, airy summit block reached via a ~100-ft, highly exposed knife-edge. The route is normally done without a rope. Rock is loose in many places, so care must be taken to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below.

Pitch 1 climbs an obvious crack up the face to the 'U-notch' on the ridge; pitch 2 follows excellent cracks on the far side; pitches 3-4 are classic exposed knife-edge ridge ('B-Basin knife riding') ending in a short downclimb, after which the ridge broadens into mellow scrambling to the summit.

Approach as for Forbidden Peak from low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft). Navigate toward South Ridge approach facing Forbidden Glacier. Route-finding less obvious than North Ridge; scout carefully. Follow exposed ridge combining fourth-class scrambling with short pitches of 5.6 climbing.

Pitch 1 steps onto a detached block, then works up a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just left of the arete to a two-bolt anchor in a notch (no chains/rings). Pitch 2 traverses left from the belay past two bolts, then follows a 'choose your own adventure' line up the face, with gear mostly limited to thin cracks and horizontal seams; the upper section has some lichen.

The standard/easiest way up Hard Mox: from a high camp near the Redoubt Glacier/Depot-Redoubt divide, traverse the glacier to the saddle between the Mox Peaks and Mt. Redoubt, descend into the 'Col of the Wild,' gain the Ridge of Gendarmes, then follow ledge/gully systems (West Ledges, Gendarme Notch, East Ledges, Southeast Gullies) to a high notch just left of the summit tower. From the notch, three pitches of loose 4th-to-low-5th-class climbing lead to the top. Most of the climbing looks more intimidating than it is; if the climbing feels harder than 5.5, you are probably off route. The route is not sandbagged but is terrifically chossy.

Grade 5.3-5.7, II-III Alpine. 600 vertical feet over 6 pitches from ridge base to summit. Rock quality excellent. Primary hazards: high exposure, significant glacier crevasses, late-season ice conditions, Class 4 downclimbing. 60m rope required for descent rappels. Often requires bivy camp due to multi-day approach.

value.text: A 60 m rope for the descent rappels.

moves.from: Accessible via Sulphide Glacier or Fisher Chimneys approaches.

beta_new: Starts up the Direct East Buttress, busting left of its bolt-ladder pitch onto a funky 5.10a section; rock quality improves through the headwall pitches, which feature sustained thin cracks starting in a corner and staying difficult for several pitches; the crux is an 5.11d pitch near the route's end. Belay locations are described as somewhat ambiguous/unmarked in the field.
A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit.

moves.from: , reached via a long glaciated approach from the Eldorado trailhead

beta_new: The 1975 first-ascent party climbed the buttress in 22 pitches over three days using titanium pitons and early Abalakov-style protection; a 2012 ascent using modern gear and 200-ft ropes compressed it to roughly 14 pitches plus 4 belay moves. The route features a major horizontal ledge at half height that is key to the line, a cave belay mid-crux, and three consecutive pitches near 5.10a/b as the technical crux, with much of the remainder in the 5.6-5.9 range. Rock is meta-granitic but includes sections of loose red rock; that party took just under 12 hours from the buttress base to the Southwest Peak. A long route (14 pitches of full 60m/200ft length on the 2012 ascent; the 1975 FA logged 22 pitches).

Most parties approach via Phelps Creek Trail to Leroy Basin, cross the Leroy High Route to Ice Lakes, camp at Lower or Upper Ice Lake, then descend and traverse into the basin between North and South Spectacle Butte before climbing the Southwest Ridge to the south summit. The line is a straightforward Class 3 ridge scramble, but the ridge crest is broken by loose gendarmes that force route-finding onto ledges and a short chossy chute/dike passage that some parties rate closer to Class 4.

The South Ridge ("Spirited Away", IV 5.9, established by Sam Boyce & Joe Manning, July 2022) climbs 12 pitches up Spectre's south ridge from Pickle Pass: sustained 5.4-5.8 crest climbing past an overhanging 5.9R choss crux (P3), through a shattered gendarme requiring a short rappel-and-reclimb (P7), and finishing through narrow hoodoo towers before a ~30m rappel and a 600-ft scramble to the summit.

Starts with two pitches on the slabby face just left of a small, deteriorating pocket glacier under the large gully on the east face. Above the slab, the face forces you left over a small rock wall, then continues straight up for a couple more pitches through brush and small trees. The route then narrows and traverses right on a narrow, jungle-filled ledge with significant exposure down the main gully; after about 50 ft, when clean rock appears above, head straight up it and belay as soon as possible to avoid rope drag (or belay on the ledge itself). Another half pitch gains the upper SE ridge, from which you scramble around to the right to reach the top. The first-ascent party took 7-8 hours on the route and arrived at the summit after dark, bivying there.

From the broad saddle between Sperry and Vesper Peaks, follow the west ridge/west slope upward -- easy at first, but above a down-sloping talus and heather bench the route steepens and the exposure increases into sustained Class 3-4 terrain to the summit. Many parties combine Sperry with adjacent Vesper Peak from the same saddle in one long day.

moves.from: Hike the Sunrise Mine Trail from its trailhead through Wirtz Basin to Headlee Pass, traverse below Sperry's south ridge past Lake Elan (Vesper Lake), then scramble up slabs to the broad saddle between Sperry and Vesper Peaks.

beta_new: The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.

moves.from: Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge.

beta_new: From a high camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col, cross the Middle Cascade Glacier to the col, descend briefly onto its south side, and traverse east under snow to a steep, narrow gully immediately right (east) of a central buttress on Spider's south/southeast face. The gully is choked with loose rock and has small Class 3 steps; most parties exit early onto the buttress (left) or a rib (right) rather than following it to its top. From the buttress/rib, gain the ridge east of the summit and traverse west (Class 3, staying south of the corniced crest) to the top. The rock is schist and notoriously rotten.

An all off-trail alpine scramble of roughly 6 miles and about 5,000 ft of elevation gain from the FR63 roadside parking to the summit. Sustained bushwhacking and blowdown low down give way to a cliff-band bypass and a snow/scree gully, ending with an exposed, sometimes loose ridge scramble with two short sections of 4th/low-5th-class climbing where a rope is often carried. It is one of the least-climbed of the Everett-area Pin Peaks, and sees sparse recent traffic.
